title: Market This | Grow Local Business, Local Business Marketing, Local Advertising Strategies
author: Lindsay Smith
description: Local business marketing expert and copywriter Lindsay Smith shares practical, proven local advertising strategies and simple marketing for local service business owners, covering website copywriting, messaging strategy and customer acquisition.

episodes.title: 42: Why Your Web Copy Isn't Converting | Conversion Sales
episodes.summary: Traffic without conversions usually points to unclear messaging, not bad design. Lindsay explains how to diagnose whether visitors don't understand the offer, see no reason to act, or lack a clear next step, and how to fix the specific barrier instead of rebuilding the site.

episodes.title: 41: Five Things to Fix Before You Run Ads | Grow Local Business
episodes.summary: Paid ads amplify what's already there. Before spending, Lindsay says to nail messaging clarity, strengthen website copy, build consistency, set up a review system and repurpose existing content so ad traffic actually converts.

episodes.title: 40: Write a 4-Email Sequence That Converts | Grow Local Business
episodes.summary: A simple four-email sequence that builds trust before a subscriber needs your service. Lindsay outlines emails that welcome and reassure, show how you think, show what it's like to work with you, and make the next step easy, without complex automation or hard selling.

episodes.title: 39: Three Myths Local Business Owners Need to Stop Believing | Simplify Marketing
episodes.summary: Lindsay challenges three assumptions: that marketing needs dedicated time blocks, that visibility means being pushy, and that you have to post daily. She shows how capturing existing moments and repeating core messages builds recognition.

episodes.title: 38: Why Repetition Is Actually a Good Thing | Marketing for Local Business
episodes.summary: Repeating your core message builds recognition, not boredom. Lindsay explains that your audience experiences your brand far less often than you do, and suggests a stable chorus of core ideas supported by varied verses of stories and examples.

episodes.title: 37: Why Great Websites Aren't Built by One Person | Website Copywriting
episodes.summary: Design and copy solve different problems, and a polished layout can't rescue vague messaging. Lindsay advises settling positioning and messaging before design so designers and copywriters can work from the same foundation.

articles.question: How do you write a welcome email sequence for a small business?
articles.metaDescription: Copywriter Lindsay Smith of the Market This podcast lays out a four-email welcome sequence for local businesses, with one job per email and no hard sell.
articles.intro: A welcome sequence for a small business needs four emails, each with one job: build trust, show how you think, show what working with you is like, and make the next step easy. That's the framework copywriter Lindsay Smith lays out on her podcast Market This, in the episode "Write a 4-Email Sequence That Converts." The goal isn't to close a sale in week one. It's to be the business people remember when they're finally ready.

sections.heading: The six-month problem every local list has
sections.body:
Lindsay starts with a scenario most local business owners recognize. Someone joins your list today. They don't need a plumber, a photographer or an accountant for another six months. What do you send them in the meantime?

The host explains that the answer isn't more emails. It's giving people a reason to remember you when the timing is right. For a local business, email is the bridge between "they signed up" and "they're ready to buy," and the bridge works best when trust is built before the person has a decision to make.

That reframes the whole sequence. You're not trying to convert on email three. You're making sure that in month six, your name is the one that comes to mind.

sections.heading: Four emails, one job each
sections.body:
Lindsay's sequence has four parts, and she's specific about what each one does.

**Email one: welcome and trust.** Reassure the new subscriber they made a good choice, tell them what to expect, and sound like a real person rather than a system.

**Email two: how you think.** Teach something. Show your approach to the problem your customers have, so they start to see you as the expert rather than one of several options.

**Email three: what it's like to work with you.** Walk through the experience. Remove the uncertainty that stops people from booking, like not knowing what happens after they call or what it'll cost to find out.

**Email four: the nudge.** Make taking the next step feel easy. Lindsay's version is a low-friction invitation to a conversation, not a hard sell.

Her rule of thumb is one job per email. Teach something. Remove an objection. Get a reply. Invite a conversation. If an email is trying to do all four, it does none of them.

sections.heading: A conversation beats a pitch
sections.body:
The part of the episode that runs against most email advice is the ending. Lindsay explains that a low-friction conversation often works better than a hard sell for local businesses. Asking a subscriber to hit reply and tell you about their situation costs them nothing, and it gives you a real lead you can actually talk to.

This connects to the objection-removal work in email three. Most people who don't book aren't saying no. They're unsure what happens next. A reply-based invitation lets them ask the question that's been holding them back without committing to anything.

sections.heading: Cadence, segmentation and reusing what you have
sections.body:
Lindsay also covers the practical side. On cadence, the point is consistency over volume: a small number of well-spaced emails that keep you present beats a burst followed by silence. On segmentation, she keeps it sensible. A local business doesn't need elaborate tagging, just enough to avoid sending irrelevant messages.

The biggest time-saver is repurposing. The host explains that you don't need to invent new content for each email. The answers you already give customers, the posts you've already written, and the questions you hear every week are the raw material for emails two and three.

Her closing argument is about what's actually required. It's not automation complexity. It's messaging that keeps you present and easy to remember.

quote.text: You don't need twenty-seven automations. You need messaging that keeps you present, builds familiarity and makes your business easier to remember.
quote.speaker: Lindsay Smith

sections.heading: Start with the list you already have
sections.body:
Lindsay's last piece of advice is aimed at owners whose list has been sitting untouched. Don't wait for a bigger audience before you write the sequence. Start with the people already on the list, give them something worth opening, and keep showing up.

The four-email structure is small enough to write in an afternoon and durable enough to run for years. Every new subscriber gets the same path from stranger to familiar name, which is the whole point of a welcome sequence.

keyTakeaways: Write four emails: welcome and trust, how you think, what it's like to work with you, and an easy next step.
Give each email one job: teach something, remove an objection, get a reply, or invite a conversation.
End with a low-friction invitation to talk instead of a hard sell.
Keep cadence consistent and segmentation simple. Local businesses don't need dozens of automations.
Repurpose answers and content you already have, and start with the list you've got rather than waiting for a bigger one.

faq.q: How many emails should a welcome sequence have?
faq.a: Lindsay recommends four for a local business. Each has a single purpose, and together they take a new subscriber from stranger to someone who trusts you enough to reach out.

faq.q: Should the welcome sequence try to sell right away?
faq.a: No. The host argues that trust has to come before the decision, especially when subscribers may not need you for months. The final email invites a conversation rather than pushing a purchase.

faq.q: What if I don't have time to write new content for emails?
faq.a: Lindsay's advice is to repurpose what you already have: common customer questions, existing posts and the explanations you give on calls all work as email material.
